interface.name: gyro_scene_v1

description.summary: where the windows are, said by the shell

interface.description:
A shell arranges the windows of its session: it groups them into containers, decides where each one goes and how big each one is, says what state each one is in, and says what kind of change every batch of that is. The compositor owns what the change looks like.
That division is the whole of this protocol. A shell may invent any arrangement - a grid, a ring, a stack of cards, a fisheye dock - and it may not invent a motion. What a person gets from that is two desktops built on this compositor that look nothing alike and feel like the same machine, because everything on both of them accelerates, overshoots and settles identically. A shell that could write its own springs would be a shell whose overview animates a little differently from the launcher beside it, and nobody would be able to say why the machine felt cheap.
So there is no request here that carries a duration, a curve, a damping ratio or a frame. What a shell says is a destination and a name for the kind of change, and the compositor decides how the world gets there.
Everything a shell says is double-buffered and applied by commit, and a commit carries the timestamp of the input event behind it. That timestamp is the point of it rather than a detail: two clients answering the same keystroke name the same instant, so the compositor composes their separate commits into one gesture, and a commit that arrives a frame late renders already in progress by exactly the right amount instead of starting late.
What an application asks for arrives here as an event rather than being decided by the compositor. Maximizing, restoring, going fullscreen and going away are window management, so a titlebar button and a video player's fullscreen control both end up as a question this shell answers - and a shell that answers none of them says so once, so that no application draws a control that does nothing.
Every object here belongs to a client the compositor has granted the run of a session, and an application is never offered this global. A client able to move other people's windows is a client able to hide the one somebody is typing into.

request.name: destroy
request.description:
Destroys the object, releasing placement if this client had claimed it - so the compositor goes back to placing windows itself, exactly as it does while no shell is running.
Containers are not affected and do not go away. They belong to the compositor, and outliving the shell that asked for them is what they are for: see get_container.
Anything staged and not yet committed is discarded.

request.name: claim_placement
request.description:
Says that this client decides where a new window of this session goes. Until it does, the compositor places windows itself, centred on the screen holding the pointer.
A window is invisible until it is placed, so this is not a preference the compositor can be wrong about while the shell catches up: a shell that claims placement and then never places anything gets a session where nothing appears. That is deliberate, and the alternative is worse - a window shown where the compositor guessed and then jumped to where the shell wanted it, on every window a person ever opens.
A shell that has claimed placement is told about new windows through ext_foreign_toplevel_list_v1, the same way it learns about every other window, and answers with place_window.
Only one client may hold this at a time, and a second claim is the placement_taken error. Unlike a claimed chord, which several clients may hold at once because a keystroke can be told to all of them, placement has exactly one answer - two placers would be a window put in two places in one frame. Failing loudly is the point: a shell that silently did not place would look to a person like a compositor that had stopped opening windows.
Placement is released when this object is destroyed or the client goes away, which is what lets the compositor keep a session usable across a shell restart.

request.name: set_capabilities

description.summary: say which window states this shell will honour

request.description:
Says which of the states below this shell actually implements, so that the applications of this session are told what their window controls may offer. Applies immediately rather than at the next commit: it is not a change to anything on screen, it is a standing statement about what this shell does.
Until a shell says otherwise it offers nothing, and that is the right default rather than a cautious one. A toolkit that is told a capability exists draws the button for it, and a button that does nothing is worse than an absent one - a person clicks it, the window does not move, and the machine looks broken rather than opinionated. So a session with no shell, or one whose shell has not spoken, gets titlebars with no controls on them, which is exactly what it can do.
A capability declared here is a promise to answer the matching window_request event. Nothing enforces that and nothing can: a shell that offers maximize and then ignores every request for it produces a dead button by hand. What the compositor can do is never invent the promise on a shell's behalf, and that is what this request is.
Bits this compositor does not know are ignored rather than being an error, because a capability is a statement about the shell rather than a request of the compositor - a newer shell offering more than this compositor can carry should lose the extra rather than the session.
There is no window-menu capability, and the omission is deliberate. There is no event here that would forward the request a client sends after it, so offering it would produce precisely the dead button the paragraph above refuses. It arrives with the event, not before it.

request.name: get_container
request.description:
Creates a container - a node with a position and a visibility of its own, which windows can be put into and which moves everything in it when it moves. A workspace, an overview grid, a stack.
The name is the shell's to mint, and it is what makes the container survive the shell. Containers belong to the compositor, not to the client that asked for one: a shell that crashes and respawns calls this again with the same names and gets the same containers back, with the same windows still in them and still where they were. What that spares a person is re-sorting forty windows after a crash they did not cause.
So this creates or re-adopts, and the state event says which happened by reporting the position and visibility the container actually has. For a new container that is what was asked for here. For one that was already there it is what survived, and the arguments to this request are ignored.
The position is where the container sits, and it is applied immediately rather than at the next commit - a container being born has nowhere to move from, so there is nothing for a transition to describe. This is the only place in this protocol where a shell states a position that does not animate, and it is the reason commit has no way to ask for no animation.
Containers are created in the session's floor, which is the compositor's own container that everything hangs under. They cannot be nested inside each other yet.
An empty name, or one longer than 256 bytes, is the bad_name error: a container that cannot be named is one that cannot be re-adopted, which defeats the point of having asked for it.

arg.name: name
arg.summary: the shell's own name for it, stable across restarts

arg.name: x
arg.summary: position, if this call creates it

arg.name: y
arg.summary: position, if this call creates it

arg.name: z
arg.summary: position, if this call creates it

request.name: place_window
request.description:
Says where a window goes and what it is in. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next commit.
A null container puts the window on the session's floor, which is where it already is if nothing has moved it. A shell with no containers at all uses this and nothing else.
The first placement of a window is its entrance. The position lands rather than animating - there is nowhere for a window to travel from before it has been anywhere - and the compositor then plays the window opening at the commit's timestamp. The transition named on that commit is not consulted for this window, because what an arriving window does is the compositor's to decide and getting it wrong is the most visible frame in the system. What the timestamp is for is that the entrance starts when the person pressed the key, not when the shell got round to answering.
Every later placement of the same window is an ordinary move under the commit's transition.
A window whose client has already closed it - a handle that has received ext_foreign_toplevel_handle_v1.closed - is silently ignored rather than being an error. An application quitting while the shell is mid-commit is ordinary, and a shell cannot avoid the race by being careful.

arg.name: container
arg.summary: what to put it in, or null for the session's floor

request.name: set_window_size

description.summary: say how big a window should be

request.description:
Says what size to ask this window to be. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next commit.
This is a request to the application rather than a change to the world, and the difference is the whole of why resizing looks the way it does everywhere. The compositor asks; the application draws a buffer at whatever size it can actually be - a terminal rounds to whole character cells, a dialog refuses to go below its own minimum - and the window's extent changes when that buffer arrives and at no other moment. A shell that treats this as a setting will find windows that are not the size it set, and every one of those is an application exercising a right the window protocol gives it.
Zero in either axis is "pick your own size", which is what every window starts at and what hands a maximized window back its natural size when it is restored. It is not the same as asking for a window of no width.
A negative width or height is the bad_size error. Zero is meaningful and negative is a shell that has subtracted a panel's height from a screen it got wrong, and clamping it quietly would leave a window at some arbitrary minimum with nothing anywhere naming the disagreement.
The size is clamped to whatever minimum and maximum the application itself declared, because those arrive from the party being resized and are the one constraint it is entitled to state.
What this does not do is animate. A window's size follows its application's next buffer, so there is nothing here for a transition to govern - where the window *is* animates, under place_window and the commit's transition, and how big it is arrives. A shell maximizing a window states both in one commit and the compositor starts the travel at once.

arg.name: width
arg.summary: width in logical pixels, or zero for the window's own

arg.name: height
arg.summary: height in logical pixels, or zero for the window's own

request.name: set_window_states
request.description:
Says which of the states below this window is in. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next commit, alongside whatever size and position were stated with it.
The whole set is stated at once rather than one bit at a time, because that is what the application is told: the state is an array on every configure, so a shell that could set one bit would still be choosing the value of all of them. Sending the set is the honest spelling of what happens on the wire.
These are declarations, not instructions. Saying a window is maximized does not resize it - set_window_size does that, and a shell that sets the state without the size gets an application that draws its maximized chrome at its old size. The pair is what a maximize is, which is why they share a commit.
What is here is exactly the states a shell decides. Whether a window has the keyboard, whether it is being resized right now, and whether nobody is looking at it are facts the compositor holds and tells the application itself, and a shell that could set them would be able to give a window a focused titlebar it does not have.
Bits this compositor does not know are ignored, for set_capabilities' reason.

arg.name: states
arg.summary: every state this window is in

request.name: commit

description.summary: apply everything staged, as one change

request.description:
Applies everything staged since the last commit, as one change of one named kind, starting at one instant.
Everything in one commit shares that instant, so a workspace sliding out and the window being focused inside it start together whatever order the requests were sent in. Everything in one commit is also seen at once: no frame is ever drawn with half of it applied.
The transition is the name of what kind of change this is, and it is the only thing a shell says about motion. The compositor holds a table of springs per transition per property, so naming one is naming a whole coordinated motion rather than a setting - and a property added to that table later starts animating at every shell that already exists, without any of them being changed.
There is deliberately no way to say "no transition". Every change a shell makes is a change a person is watching, and the state a shell wants to set without motion - where a container sits when it is first made - is stated at get_container instead, before there is anything on screen to move. Left available, a shell could set a position with no animation sixty times a second and hand-animate the desktop itself, which is exactly the cohesion this protocol exists to hold.
The timestamp is the instant the input event behind this change was reported by its device, on CLOCK_MONOTONIC - the same value gyro_binding_v1.pressed carries, and the reason that event carries it. For a change no input event is behind, such as a monitor being plugged in, the shell's own clock reading is correct and honest. A timestamp later than the compositor's own reading of the clock is treated as now, because a change stamped into the future is one that stands still until the clock catches up, which reads as the machine having hung.
A transition this compositor does not know is the bad_transition error. A commit with nothing staged is legal and does nothing.

arg.name: transition
arg.summary: the kind of change this is

arg.name: tv_sec_hi
arg.summary: high 32 bits of the seconds part of the timestamp

arg.name: tv_sec_lo
arg.summary: low 32 bits of the seconds part of the timestamp

event.name: work_area

description.summary: the part of a screen a window should be put in

event.description:
The rectangle on one screen that ordinary windows belong inside: the output, less whatever chrome has reserved space along its edges.
Sent once per output when this object is created, and again whenever the rectangle moves - a monitor plugged in or unplugged, a screen rearranged, a panel appearing or changing height. An output this client has not bound as a wl_output cannot be named, so nothing is sent for it until the client binds one, at which point the event it missed arrives.
The coordinates are in the same space as place_window on a window with no container, which is what makes this directly useful: maximizing a window is placing it at this origin and asking it to be this size.
Why the compositor holds this rather than the shell working it out: the panel reserving the space and the shell placing the windows are separate processes, and they should stay that way - a bug in a status bar should not take window management with it. The compositor is the only party that sees both, so it does the arithmetic and says the answer once.
This is also what a window is told it has room for when it opens, so an application picks its first size against the same rectangle a shell would maximize it into. An application that opens underneath the panel is what happens when those two disagree.
A fullscreen window deliberately ignores this and covers the whole output. That is what fullscreen means, and it is why the two states are not the same request with a different number.

event.name: window_request

description.summary: an application asked for a window state

event.description:
An application has asked to be maximized, restored, fullscreened or minimized. It is asking this shell, because deciding is window management and the compositor does not do that.
This is what makes a titlebar's buttons and a video player's fullscreen control work at all. An application that asks and hears nothing is not an application that has been refused - it is one still waiting, holding its own transition open. That is the failure this event exists to prevent, and its shape is a browser whose fullscreen button does nothing at all: the page's own fullscreen event never fires, and a person clicking the control on a video sees the frame they were already looking at.
So a shell that has declared a capability owes an answer to every request for it. The answer is set_window_states with the new set, and set_window_size beside it, on a commit. Refusing is an answer too, and it is spelled by stating the states the window already has - the application then reads the state it asked for as absent and puts its own interface back.
Only the client holding placement is told, since it is the only one that could answer. A request that reaches nobody - no shell, or one that never claimed placement - is answered by the compositor with the window exactly as it is, which is the same refusal spelled by the only party left to spell it.
The output is the screen the application would prefer to be fullscreen on, and it is null for every other request and for a client with no preference. It is a preference rather than an instruction: which screen a window is on is placement, and placement is this shell's.
The timestamp is when the compositor received the request, on CLOCK_MONOTONIC, in the encoding commit reads. Echo it back on the commit that answers, so the window starts moving from the moment the person clicked rather than from the moment the answer was worked out. It is not the instant of the click itself - no application says when it was clicked - and it is the earliest moment anything here knows about.

arg.name: output
arg.summary: the screen it would prefer, for fullscreen, or null

arg.name: tv_sec_hi
arg.summary: high 32 bits of the seconds part of the timestamp

arg.name: tv_sec_lo
arg.summary: low 32 bits of the seconds part of the timestamp

enum.name: transition

description.summary: the kinds of change the compositor knows how to draw

enum.description:
A closed set, and it grows by the compositor learning a new kind of change rather than by a client describing one. Each name stands for a coordinated motion across every property it touches, designed as one thing.
There is no entry for "none", and commit says why.

entry.name: window_open
entry.summary: a window arriving

entry.name: window_close
entry.summary: a window leaving

entry.name: menu_appear
entry.summary: a menu or popup opening

entry.name: menu_dismiss
entry.summary: a menu or popup closing

entry.name: workspace_switch
entry.summary: moving between workspaces

entry.name: focus_change
entry.summary: attention moving from one window to another

entry.name: matched_move
entry.summary: something travelling from where it was to where it now is

entry.name: background_change
entry.summary: the desktop behind everything changing

enum.name: state

description.summary: what a window is, as far as its application is concerned

enum.description:
The states a shell decides and an application is told about. Absent from this list, and deliberately: whether a window has the keyboard, whether it is being resized at this instant, and whether nobody is looking at it. Those are the compositor's own facts about a window, and a shell able to set them could give a window a focused titlebar it does not have.
Minimized is not here either, and the reason is that the window protocol has no such state - there is nothing to tell an application and no way for it to observe the result. A shell minimizes a window by putting it somewhere nobody is looking, which is a container it has hidden.

entry.name: maximized
entry.summary: filling the work area

entry.name: fullscreen
entry.summary: filling the whole output, over everything

entry.name: tiled_left
entry.summary: its left edge is against something

entry.name: tiled_right
entry.summary: its right edge is against something

entry.name: tiled_top
entry.summary: its top edge is against something

entry.name: tiled_bottom
entry.summary: its bottom edge is against something

enum.name: capability
enum.description: What an application may show a control for. See set_capabilities: a capability is a promise to answer the matching window_request.

entry.name: maximize
entry.summary: this shell answers maximize and unmaximize

entry.name: minimize
entry.summary: this shell answers minimize

entry.name: fullscreen
entry.summary: this shell answers fullscreen and unfullscreen

enum.name: action
enum.description: Not a bitfield: an application asks for one thing at a time, and a request to be maximized and unmaximized at once is not a thing it can mean.

entry.name: maximize
entry.summary: fill the work area

entry.name: unmaximize
entry.summary: go back to what it was

entry.name: fullscreen
entry.summary: fill the screen

entry.name: unfullscreen
entry.summary: stop filling the screen

entry.name: minimize
entry.summary: go away without closing

entry.name: placement_taken
entry.summary: another client is already placing this session's windows

entry.name: bad_name
entry.summary: the container name is empty or too long

entry.name: bad_transition
entry.summary: the transition is not one this compositor knows

entry.name: bad_size
entry.summary: a window size had a negative width or height

interface.name: gyro_container_v1
interface.description:
A container the compositor holds on this shell's behalf: a position, a visibility, and whatever has been placed inside it. Moving it moves everything in it as one, which is what a workspace switch is.
It is the compositor's rather than the client's, so this object is a reference to it and not the thing itself. Destroying the object leaves the container standing; remove is how a container actually goes away.

request.name: destroy
request.description:
Destroys this object. The container itself is untouched, along with everything in it.
That is the opposite of what destroying an object usually means, and it is the whole reason containers are named. A shell exits or crashes and every object it held is destroyed; if that took the containers with it, a crash would dissolve every workspace in the session and pile forty windows into one heap. Instead the panel blinks out and comes back, and the arrangement it comes back to is the one the person left.
Anything staged on this container and not yet committed is discarded.

request.name: remove
request.description:
Removes the container. Anything still in it returns to the session's floor, at the position it had inside the container, so a window is never left with nowhere to be.
This object stays valid and inert afterwards, and every request on it does nothing; the client should destroy it.
This is the deliberate act, as against destroy above. A person closing a workspace does this; a shell exiting does not.

request.name: set_position
request.description:
Sets where the container sits. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next gyro_scene_v1.commit, under that commit's transition.
Everything in the container moves with it, as one thing rather than as several - which is what makes a workspace switch a single sliding surface instead of a dozen windows travelling in loose formation.

request.name: set_visible
request.description:
Shows or hides the container and everything under it. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next gyro_scene_v1.commit.
Hiding is immediate and does not animate, whatever the commit says: there is nothing between shown and hidden to draw. A shell that wants a workspace to fade out moves it or fades it under a transition and hides it afterwards.
A hidden container still holds its windows, still keeps their positions, and still costs the compositor nothing to skip.

event.name: state
event.description:
Sent once, immediately after the container is created or re-adopted, and never again.
For a container this call created, it repeats what was asked for. For one that was already there, it is what survived - which is how a shell that has just restarted learns that its workspaces are where it left them rather than where it would have put them.
What this does not yet carry is what is in the container. A restarted shell knows its containers are back and does not know which window is in which, so it cannot redraw a workspace strip without asking every window where it is. That is missing rather than withheld.
